content.content:
1	WRD-1 | A button or menu item is a command: it starts with a specific verb that names what happens (connect, install; not configure, manage or set), named for what the reader wants done, not the technology. Its words tell it apart from its neighbours: paired opposites (Add and Remove, Show and Hide), a modifier for similar commands (Insert row above, Insert row below), the object it acts on (Open Windows Defender), singular or plural by how many things it acts on.
2	  W: Standard labels without a verb are accepted: OK, Yes, No, About, Advanced, Back, Details, Forward, Full screen, Less, More, New, Next, Options, Personalize, Previous, Properties, Settings. A noun stands alone where the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage (Tools, Page, Status bar). A verb that repeats the menu title is dropped (Insert > Table). When every answer in a set starts with the same words, they are dropped from all. Background work is Suspend/Resume, anything else Enable/Disable.
3	  M: The verb stays where Windows drops it (Show Toolbar, Enter Full Screen); verbless labels only for the standard noun commands (Settings…, About <App>, Bold).
4	  now: none - No check on label wording (`uitest/uitest.go:194-212` checks only that a name exists). The library's own strings are verb-first (`table.go:595-605`, `duallist.go:54-57`).
5	WRD-2 | Keep a command label to one to three words, using only the words the command needs; a word more is better than a separate explanation.
6	  W: A labelled toolbar button may have up to four words. When specific answer labels would reach five words or more, ask a yes-or-no question instead (WRD-7) or give the answers as command links (see open question on command links).
7	  now: none - No length check (`button.go:119-123` grows the button to any text). The library's own labels break it: "Move the selected column earlier" (`duallist.go:56`), "Select every row the current filter shows" (`table.go:843`).
8	WRD-3 | Leave articles and possessives off labels, menu items and tooltips.
9	  now: contradicts - Library defaults carry articles: "Clear the filter" (`searchfield.go:56`), "Close the pane" (`pane.go:44`), "Dismiss this notice" (`feedback.go:261`), "Clear the sort" (`table.go:597`).
10	WRD-4 | A command that needs more input before it acts (a dialog that asks, a chooser, a confirmation) ends with an ellipsis (…); one that acts at once, or opens a submenu, has none.
11	  W: A command whose whole job is to show a window has no ellipsis, even if that window holds settings: About, Advanced, Help, Options, Properties, Settings, Sharing settings. A command followed only by a confirmation has one. An icon-only toolbar button that asks for more has the ellipsis in its tooltip (Print…); toolbar commands should mostly act at once. Help links never end in an ellipsis. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
12	  M: Ellipsis character U+2026, not three full stops. Settings… and other commands that open a window to collect input take it.
13	  now: partly - Written by hand ("Open &Folder…" in the doc at `menu.go:22`); nothing adds or checks it (survey §15).
14	WRD-6 | Capitalise each kind of text in the platform's style, and give every label of one kind the same style across the app. Capitalise feature names sparingly and consistently; generic words (toolbar, menu, button, icon) stay lower case.
15	  W: Title case only for titles: window and dialog titles, a guided flow's name, without ending punctuation. Everything else is sentence case: menu titles and items, buttons, command links, tabs, column headings, field, check box, radio, list and slider labels, list options and data, prompts, links, tooltips, toolbar labels, palette titles, main instructions, supplemental text, progress text and balloon titles.
16	  M: Title case: menu items and menu titles, buttons, tabs, segment labels, column headings, panel titles, notification titles and buttons. Sentence case: tooltips, alert body text, box titles, field and slider labels, notification body. Alert buttons: open question Q-3.
17	  now: partly - Library strings are sentence case throughout (survey §14), which is the Windows form; there is no title-case conversion for macOS and no check (survey §15).
18	WRD-7 | A confirming button names the action it confirms (Insert, Import), never a generic word such as Confirm; what people must notice about the action goes on the button itself (Format disk, not OK under a paragraph about formatting). When the dialog gives a reason not to go ahead, the button adds anyway (Install anyway). Now and later appear only to tell doing it at once from doing it later.
19	  W: OK, Yes and No appear only in these cases, spelled OK (never Ok or Okay). OK commits a window that changes settings or properties rather than doing one task (OK, Cancel, Apply). Yes and No answer a question phrased as yes or no, always as a pair, never replaced by OK and Cancel, and only when specific answers would be long or awkward or the reader must read the question (a risky-action confirmation). A message with no action of its own has a single Close button, never OK. When an error ends the program the button is Exit program. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
20	  M: Never OK, Yes or No on a confirming button, except OK in an informing alert with one button (Q-4).
21	  now: contradicts - Dialog defaults ConfirmText to "Confirm" (`feedback.go:424`), the generic word the rule forbids; an informing dialog needs CancelText set to "" by hand (`feedback.go:452`) and has no Close-only form.
22	WRD-8 | The button that abandons the action is Cancel, and Cancel leaves no trace. Once something cannot be undone it becomes Close (the work is done, or the window only shows things) or Stop (work is running and what is done is kept); Escape presses it.
23	  W: Cancel turns into Close once a step has run or applied changes that cannot be undone (and back to Cancel after Apply), and into Stop once going back is no longer possible mid-operation. A modeless dialog has Close, never Cancel. Yes never pairs with Cancel alone (Yes/No/Cancel is allowed). When several pending actions make it unclear what Cancel would cancel, or only the dialog itself can be declined, a specific negative answer replaces it (Don't run). Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
24	  M: Cancel is never renamed; a specific negative answer (Don't Save) sits beside Cancel, not in its place.
25	  now: partly - CancelText defaults to "Cancel" (`feedback.go:424`) and FloatingView's close is "Close" (`floatingview.go:61`); nothing switches Cancel to Close or Stop, and Progress has no halt button (survey §8).
26	WRD-9 | A New command names the kind of thing it makes.
27	  now: none - Not covered.
28	WRD-10 | Delete removes without touching the clipboard and matches the Delete key; Cut copies then removes. Do not call removal Erase or Clear, and do not call a move to the trash Delete without saying so.
29	  now: none - Not covered.
30	WRD-11 | Undo and Redo name the action they reverse.
31	  now: none - No undo stack (survey §13).
32	WRD-12 | A command that switches a state says unmistakably what it does in each state.
33	  W: A menu item keeps its name whatever the state and shows the state with a tick (on or off) or a bullet (one of several modes): "Status bar" with a tick, not "Show status bar" turning into "Hide status bar". Items named after objects (recent files, open windows) may change. A tray menu item stays enabled and shows its state with a tick.
34	  M: The words change with the state: Show Sidebar / Hide Sidebar; a tick only for attributes (CMD-15).
35	  now: partly - MenuItem `Checked` draws a tick (`menu.go:40-42`), which is the Windows form; there is no word swap for macOS, and TrayItem has no check (`platform/tray.go:49-60`).
36	WRD-13 | A tooltip is short, concerns only its control, does not repeat a visible label, and never says how to operate the control (right-click to…).
37	  W: A tooltip on an unlabelled control is its label: the command name in sentence case, plus the shortcut and any default in parentheses (Bold (Ctrl+B)), and an ellipsis when the command asks for more. A descriptive tip on an item (infotip) is complete sentences in the present tense, with full stops, in short parts. A notification-area icon's tip gives the program's name and, if useful, a short status, without version numbers. The Start menu description is at most 25 words, starts with a specific verb, lists the main tasks in the words people search for, without catch-alls or marketing, in sentence case. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
38	  M: A fragment starting with a verb that says what the control does: no articles, no full stop, sentence case, within about 60 characters.
39	  now: partly - IconButton's tooltip is Label plus Explanation on a line of its own (`iconbutton.go:69-74`, `control.go:392-409`), the Windows shape without the shortcut; no length limit (`control.go:402-403`); the tray tooltip is free text (`platform/tray.go:207-208`).
40	WRD-14 | Speak to the reader as you; never call them the user; say you can, not the app lets you. In a problem message, do not make the reader the culprit: leave out you and use the passive where the active would blame. We only for the maker, sparingly (Q-8).
41	  W: An answer the reader picks (a command link or an option) may speak as the reader in the first person, and is then exempt from WRD-3 (Print the photos on my camera). We recommend is preferred to it is recommended.
42	  now: none - Not covered.
43	WRD-15 | Use plain words in the reader's terms: what they want to do, not the technology behind it. One clear word where one will do (lock, not lock down; because, not since), short product names without trademarks or versions, accurate statements; no jargon without a definition, idioms, slang, jokes or exclamations such as Oops. Short fragments are fine where they read naturally.
44	  now: none - Not covered.
45	WRD-16 | Write without gender where it is irrelevant, and never use a disability as a metaphor.
46	  now: none - Not covered.
47	WRD-17 | Name the action for the input in use: click on the desktop, never tap; press a key, type text, hold a key kept down, use the arrow keys; select an item in a list or a check box and clear it to uncheck. Call them keyboard shortcuts, never accelerators, mnemonics or hot keys; tab alone means a tab, otherwise the Tab key or a tab stop.
48	  W: Click for menu items and buttons, never choose, select or pick; select for list items and check boxes, enter for a value that can also be chosen from a list.
49	  M: Choose for menu items (choose File > Save), click for buttons.
50	  now: none - Not covered.
51	WRD-18 | Link text says what is behind it, in words that tell the screen's links apart; never "click here". A help link is the question its topic answers (How do I add exceptions?), the whole sentence is the link, and it says so when it goes to the web. A generic More information is acceptable only right after an instruction already on screen. An inline link keeps its sentence's capitalisation, with the full stop outside it; a link that acts at once beside one that only goes somewhere adds now.
52	  now: none - Link takes free text (`link.go:35`); nothing checks it.
53	WRD-19 | Every field, list, tree, slider and group of controls has a visible label: a word or phrase naming what it holds, not how to operate it, saying when several may be chosen or how to separate them; instructions go above the label in full sentences. A control that completes a check box or radio option uses that option's label. A prompt (placeholder) names the purpose or gives an example; it stands in for the label only in a search field or a field on a toolbar with no room, and never holds information needed while typing.
54	  W: A label beside or above its control ends with a colon (Name:), which assistive technology also uses. The prompt disappears when the field takes focus (at the first keystroke if it starts focused) and returns when the field is left empty; it is a sentence-case fragment without ending punctuation or ellipsis.
55	  M: The placeholder stays until the first keystroke.
56	  now: partly - Field.Label names the field for a screen reader only; there is no visible label or LabeledBy (`field.go:34-35`, `uitest/uitest.go:206`). No catch-all such as General, Advanced or Settings unless the page really holds common or expert-only items that fit nowhere else; a tab for a document or view carries its name. No ending punctuation. A group label says what the choice is for, and that at least one is needed when it is, not how to choose.
58	  W: A group label written as text above its controls ends with a colon (Alignment:); group box titles, tabs and column headings do not. A menu title may be a verb (Insert, Format), and is a noun when the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage. List groups by date use Today, Yesterday, Last week, Earlier this year, A long time ago.
59	  now: none - Not covered.
60	WRD-21 | A multi-step flow is named by its task (Connect to a network), never with the word wizard; every page has a main instruction (WRD-26); one advancing word is used throughout, and the flow can always be left (WIN-22).
61	  W: Next only while Back or Cancel can still undo the step. The step that commits has a specific verb answering the page's instruction (Print, Connect); Finish only when that verb would be generic (Save, Choose) or the flow only changes settings. Pages after the work is done end with Close, never Done or Cancel. Back is an unlabelled arrow at the top leading corner, with a tooltip and a name. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
62	  M: Continue (or Next) advances throughout and Done ends the flow.
63	  now: none - No wizard or flow component.
64	WRD-22 | A setting has a plain label and at most one short line saying what it does; anything longer goes behind a Hint. Explain only the options that need it, never restating a label; a short note may sit in parentheses after the label or below the control; say when a choice becomes the default for next time. Settings text describes; it does not order people about. Skippable detail goes in a footnote or behind Help.
65	  now: partly - Hint exists for long explanations (`popover.go:159-213`) and RadioGroup draws one Detail line per option (`radiogroup.go:150-153`); nothing limits or checks either.
66	WRD-23 | Call things by what the reader sees, never by implementation words (popover, pane, scene, modal, list view, text box). Help names a control by its exact label, without colon or access-key mark.
67	  W: Help adds the plain kind after the label: the Password box, the Programs list, the Underline check box, the View tab, the Screen resolution slider, the Network icon in the notification area. A settings window is a dialog box with tabs; a flow may be called the <Name> wizard. A group is named only to tell apart options with the same name (Under Effects, select Hidden). The area beside the clock is the notification area, never the system tray.
68	  M: Help refers to the control by its label or to the task, without the kind.

70	WRD-24 | Write shortcuts in the platform's form.
71	  W: Key names as printed (Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Enter, Page Up, Tab), letters in capitals, joined with + and no spaces (Ctrl+Shift+N), modifiers in the order Windows logo, Ctrl, Alt, Shift. 256	  W: Ctrl+N, O, S, P, Z, Ctrl+Y for Redo, Ctrl+X, C, V, A, F; F3 Find next, Ctrl+H Replace, Ctrl+G Go to, F1 Help (contextual help optional), F2 Rename the selection, F5 Refresh, F11 Full screen, Alt+Enter Properties of the focused object, Alt+F4 Close the window. 265	  M: Cmd-Space, Cmd-Tab, Ctrl-F1 to F7, Shift-Cmd-3/4, Opt-Cmd-Esc, Opt-Cmd-D, Ctrl-Space and Cmd-Left/Right for input sources.

A shortcut means one thing across the whole app, and an app with many shortcuts lets people reassign them.

For rarer commands: Ctrl+function key (not F4 or F6) and Ctrl+Shift+letter or digit. Commands on the selection take function keys (F2 renames); commands on the whole document take Ctrl combinations (Ctrl+S).
269	  M: The general rule, with the modifiers of KEY-3.

When a command button has keyboard focus, Enter presses that button instead. A destructive button may be the default only when its action is easy to undo. A window that appears unprompted has no default button and no access keys, and its initial focus is off the commit buttons. Other controls leave Enter to the default: a disclosure opens with Space, a drop-down arrow with Space on its own or Alt+Down inside another control.
273	  M: Return presses the default button and focus on another button does not move it; a destructive button is never the default; a dialog that must be read has no default.

275	KEY-7 | Escape cancels a dialog, popover or menu, and abandons a drag, move, resize or split in progress, putting things back; on a Mac Command-period cancels too.

WRD-1 | A button or menu item is a command: it starts with a specific verb that names what happens (connect, install; not configure, manage or set), named for what the reader wants done, not the technology. Its words tell it apart from its neighbours: paired opposites (Add and Remove, Show and Hide), a modifier for similar commands (Insert row above, Insert row below), the object it acts on (Open Windows Defender), singular or plural by how many things it acts on.
  W: Standard labels without a verb are accepted: OK, Yes, No, About, Advanced, Back, Details, Forward, Full screen, Less, More, New, Next, Options, Personalize, Previous, Properties, Settings. A noun stands alone where the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage (Tools, Page, Status bar). A verb that repeats the menu title is dropped (Insert > Table). When every answer in a set starts with the same words, they are dropped from all. Background work is Suspend/Resume, anything else Enable/Disable.
  M: The verb stays where Windows drops it (Show Toolbar, Enter Full Screen); verbless labels only for the standard noun commands (Settings…, About <App>, Bold).
  now: none - No check on label wording (`uitest/uitest.go:194-212` checks only that a name exists). The library's own strings are verb-first (`table.go:595-605`, `duallist.go:54-57`).
WRD-2 | Keep a command label to one to three words, using only the words the command needs; a word more is better than a separate explanation.
  W: A labelled toolbar button may have up to four words. When specific answer labels would reach five words or more, ask a yes-or-no question instead (WRD-7) or give the answers as command links (see open question on command links).
  now: none - No length check (`button.go:119-123` grows the button to any text). The library's own labels break it: "Move the selected column earlier" (`duallist.go:56`), "Select every row the current filter shows" (`table.go:843`).
WRD-3 | Leave articles and possessives off labels, menu items and tooltips.
  now: contradicts - Library defaults carry articles: "Clear the filter" (`searchfield.go:56`), "Close the pane" (`pane.go:44`), "Dismiss this notice" (`feedback.go:261`), "Clear the sort" (`table.go:597`).
WRD-4 | A command that needs more input before it acts (a dialog that asks, a chooser, a confirmation) ends with an ellipsis (…); one that acts at once, or opens a submenu, has none.
  W: A command whose whole job is to show a window has no ellipsis, even if that window holds settings: About, Advanced, Help, Options, Properties, Settings, Sharing settings. A command followed only by a confirmation has one. An icon-only toolbar button that asks for more has the ellipsis in its tooltip (Print…); toolbar commands should mostly act at once. Help links never end in an ellipsis. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
  M: Ellipsis character U+2026, not three full stops. Settings… and other commands that open a window to collect input take it.
  now: partly - Written by hand ("Open &Folder…" in the doc at `menu.go:22`); nothing adds or checks it (survey §15).
WRD-6 | Capitalise each kind of text in the platform's style, and give every label of one kind the same style across the app. Capitalise feature names sparingly and consistently; generic words (toolbar, menu, button, icon) stay lower case.
  W: Title case only for titles: window and dialog titles, a guided flow's name, without ending punctuation. Everything else is sentence case: menu titles and items, buttons, command links, tabs, column headings, field, check box, radio, list and slider labels, list options and data, prompts, links, tooltips, toolbar labels, palette titles, main instructions, supplemental text, progress text and balloon titles.
  M: Title case: menu items and menu titles, buttons, tabs, segment labels, column headings, panel titles, notification titles and buttons. Sentence case: tooltips, alert body text, box titles, field and slider labels, notification body. Alert buttons: open question Q-3.
  now: partly - Library strings are sentence case throughout (survey §14), which is the Windows form; there is no title-case conversion for macOS and no check (survey §15).
WRD-7 | A confirming button names the action it confirms (Insert, Import), never a generic word such as Confirm; what people must notice about the action goes on the button itself (Format disk, not OK under a paragraph about formatting). When the dialog gives a reason not to go ahead, the button adds anyway (Install anyway). Now and later appear only to tell doing it at once from doing it later.
  W: OK, Yes and No appear only in these cases, spelled OK (never Ok or Okay). OK commits a window that changes settings or properties rather than doing one task (OK, Cancel, Apply). Yes and No answer a question phrased as yes or no, always as a pair, never replaced by OK and Cancel, and only when specific answers would be long or awkward or the reader must read the question (a risky-action confirmation). A message with no action of its own has a single Close button, never OK. When an error ends the program the button is Exit program. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
  M: Never OK, Yes or No on a confirming button, except OK in an informing alert with one button (Q-4).
  now: contradicts - Dialog defaults ConfirmText to "Confirm" (`feedback.go:424`), the generic word the rule forbids; an informing dialog needs CancelText set to "" by hand (`feedback.go:452`) and has no Close-only form.
WRD-8 | The button that abandons the action is Cancel, and Cancel leaves no trace. Once something cannot be undone it becomes Close (the work is done, or the window only shows things) or Stop (work is running and what is done is kept); Escape presses it.
  W: Cancel turns into Close once a step has run or applied changes that cannot be undone (and back to Cancel after Apply), and into Stop once going back is no longer possible mid-operation. A modeless dialog has Close, never Cancel. Yes never pairs with Cancel alone (Yes/No/Cancel is allowed). When several pending actions make it unclear what Cancel would cancel, or only the dialog itself can be declined, a specific negative answer replaces it (Don't run). Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
  M: Cancel is never renamed; a specific negative answer (Don't Save) sits beside Cancel, not in its place.
  now: partly - CancelText defaults to "Cancel" (`feedback.go:424`) and FloatingView's close is "Close" (`floatingview.go:61`); nothing switches Cancel to Close or Stop, and Progress has no halt button (survey §8).
WRD-9 | A New command names the kind of thing it makes.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-10 | Delete removes without touching the clipboard and matches the Delete key; Cut copies then removes. Do not call removal Erase or Clear, and do not call a move to the trash Delete without saying so.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-11 | Undo and Redo name the action they reverse.
  now: none - No undo stack (survey §13).
WRD-12 | A command that switches a state says unmistakably what it does in each state.
  W: A menu item keeps its name whatever the state and shows the state with a tick (on or off) or a bullet (one of several modes): "Status bar" with a tick, not "Show status bar" turning into "Hide status bar". Items named after objects (recent files, open windows) may change. A tray menu item stays enabled and shows its state with a tick.
  M: The words change with the state: Show Sidebar / Hide Sidebar; a tick only for attributes (CMD-15).
  now: partly - MenuItem `Checked` draws a tick (`menu.go:40-42`), which is the Windows form; there is no word swap for macOS, and TrayItem has no check (`platform/tray.go:49-60`).
WRD-13 | A tooltip is short, concerns only its control, does not repeat a visible label, and never says how to operate the control (right-click to…).
  W: A tooltip on an unlabelled control is its label: the command name in sentence case, plus the shortcut and any default in parentheses (Bold (Ctrl+B)), and an ellipsis when the command asks for more. A descriptive tip on an item (infotip) is complete sentences in the present tense, with full stops, in short parts. A notification-area icon's tip gives the program's name and, if useful, a short status, without version numbers. The Start menu description is at most 25 words, starts with a specific verb, lists the main tasks in the words people search for, without catch-alls or marketing, in sentence case. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
  M: A fragment starting with a verb that says what the control does: no articles, no full stop, sentence case, within about 60 characters.
  now: partly - IconButton's tooltip is Label plus Explanation on a line of its own (`iconbutton.go:69-74`, `control.go:392-409`), the Windows shape without the shortcut; no length limit (`control.go:402-403`); the tray tooltip is free text (`platform/tray.go:207-208`).
WRD-14 | Speak to the reader as you; never call them the user; say you can, not the app lets you. In a problem message, do not make the reader the culprit: leave out you and use the passive where the active would blame. We only for the maker, sparingly (Q-8).
  W: An answer the reader picks (a command link or an option) may speak as the reader in the first person, and is then exempt from WRD-3 (Print the photos on my camera). We recommend is preferred to it is recommended.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-15 | Use plain words in the reader's terms: what they want to do, not the technology behind it. One clear word where one will do (lock, not lock down; because, not since), short product names without trademarks or versions, accurate statements; no jargon without a definition, idioms, slang, jokes or exclamations such as Oops. Short fragments are fine where they read naturally.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-16 | Write without gender where it is irrelevant, and never use a disability as a metaphor.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-17 | Name the action for the input in use: click on the desktop, never tap; press a key, type text, hold a key kept down, use the arrow keys; select an item in a list or a check box and clear it to uncheck. Call them keyboard shortcuts, never accelerators, mnemonics or hot keys; tab alone means a tab, otherwise the Tab key or a tab stop.
  W: Click for menu items and buttons, never choose, select or pick; select for list items and check boxes, enter for a value that can also be chosen from a list.
  M: Choose for menu items (choose File > Save), click for buttons.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-18 | Link text says what is behind it, in words that tell the screen's links apart; never "click here". A help link is the question its topic answers (How do I add exceptions?), the whole sentence is the link, and it says so when it goes to the web. A generic More information is acceptable only right after an instruction already on screen. An inline link keeps its sentence's capitalisation, with the full stop outside it; a link that acts at once beside one that only goes somewhere adds now.
  now: none - Link takes free text (`link.go:35`); nothing checks it.
WRD-19 | Every field, list, tree, slider and group of controls has a visible label: a word or phrase naming what it holds, not how to operate it, saying when several may be chosen or how to separate them; instructions go above the label in full sentences. A control that completes a check box or radio option uses that option's label. A prompt (placeholder) names the purpose or gives an example; it stands in for the label only in a search field or a field on a toolbar with no room, and never holds information needed while typing.
  W: A label beside or above its control ends with a colon (Name:), which assistive technology also uses. The prompt disappears when the field takes focus (at the first keystroke if it starts focused) and returns when the field is left empty; it is a sentence-case fragment without ending punctuation or ellipsis.
  M: The placeholder stays until the first keystroke.
  now: partly - Field.Label names the field for a screen reader only; there is no visible label or LabeledBy (`field.go:34-35`, `uitest/uitest.go:206`). The placeholder shows while the field is empty, focused or not (`field.go:344-346`), the macOS behaviour. SearchField's prompt "Filter…" ends in an ellipsis (`sear
WRD-20 | Name what a group of things is with a specific noun: column headings, tabs, segments, panel titles, sidebar groups, submenus, and menu titles (one word each in a menu bar). No catch-all such as General, Advanced or Settings unless the page really holds common or expert-only items that fit nowhere else; a tab for a document or view carries its name. No ending punctuation. A group label says what the choice is for, and that at least one is needed when it is, not how to choose.
  W: A group label written as text above its controls ends with a colon (Alignment:); group box titles, tabs and column headings do not. A menu title may be a verb (Insert, Format), and is a noun when the verb would be Create, Show, View or Manage. List groups by date use Today, Yesterday, Last week, Earlier this year, A long time ago.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-21 | A multi-step flow is named by its task (Connect to a network), never with the word wizard; every page has a main instruction (WRD-26); one advancing word is used throughout, and the flow can always be left (WIN-22).
  W: Next only while Back or Cancel can still undo the step. The step that commits has a specific verb answering the page's instruction (Print, Connect); Finish only when that verb would be generic (Save, Choose) or the flow only changes settings. Pages after the work is done end with Close, never Done or Cancel. Back is an unlabelled arrow at the top leading corner, with a tooltip and a name. Windows 7 guide; current Fluent guidance could not be fetched.
  M: Continue (or Next) advances throughout and Done ends the flow.
  now: none - No wizard or flow component.
WRD-22 | A setting has a plain label and at most one short line saying what it does; anything longer goes behind a Hint. Explain only the options that need it, never restating a label; a short note may sit in parentheses after the label or below the control; say when a choice becomes the default for next time. Settings text describes; it does not order people about. Skippable detail goes in a footnote or behind Help.
  now: partly - Hint exists for long explanations (`popover.go:159-213`) and RadioGroup draws one Detail line per option (`radiogroup.go:150-153`); nothing limits or checks either.
WRD-23 | Call things by what the reader sees, never by implementation words (popover, pane, scene, modal, list view, text box). Help names a control by its exact label, without colon or access-key mark.
  W: Help adds the plain kind after the label: the Password box, the Programs list, the Underline check box, the View tab, the Screen resolution slider, the Network icon in the notification area. A settings window is a dialog box with tabs; a flow may be called the <Name> wizard. A group is named only to tell apart options with the same name (Under Effects, select Hidden). The area beside the clock is the notification area, never the system tray.
  M: Help refers to the control by its label or to the task, without the kind.
  now: none - Not covered.
WRD-24 | Write shortcuts in the platform's form.
  W: Key names as printed (Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Enter, Page Up, Tab), letters in capitals, joined with + and no spaces (Ctrl+Shift+N), modifiers in the order Windows logo, Ctrl, Alt, Shift. A shifted punctuation key is written with Shift and the shifted character (Ctrl+Shift+?). In running text, punctuation and arrows are spelled out (Ctrl+plus sign, left arrow); never glyphs or all capitals.
  M: Glyphs ⌃⌥⇧⌘ in that order, and the shifted symbol itself (⌘?).
  now: partly - `menu.go:257` prints `it.Key.String()`. unison's neutral form writes Ctrl+, Alt+, Shift+ in the Windows order but Super+ last (unison `enums/mod/modifiers.go:100-123`), and names keys Return and PageUp (unison `keys.go:439`, `keys.go:457`), not Enter and Page Up.
WRD-25 | A progress description says exactly what is happening, never just Loading…, Working… or Please wait: an -ing phrase naming the operation, ending in an ellipsis (Printing your pictures…, Copying…). Work the reader did not start says why they wait (Please wait while …). Time remaining runs from the largest unit down, two units at most, no more precise than the estimate (hours and minutes, no seconds), singular for one (1 minute). Each progress detail has a label and a unit (Speed: 2 MB/s).
  now: contradicts - BusyText defaults to "Working…" (`button.go:73`); Progress has no time remaining (survey §8).
WRD-26 | Each dialog, page or message leads with one main instruction: what the reader should do or decide, as an imperative or a specific question in terms of their goal, in one sentence, essentials first. Leave it out where the purpose is obvious (Open, Save). Supplemental text only adds context, in short sentences, with detail behind Help; a dialog the app opened by itself says why. Say each thing once across title, instruction, text and buttons, keeping the full words in the instruction and on the controls; a control label that only repeats the instruction is dropped. A confirmation asks Are you sure you want to… only for the direct result of a request and Do you want to… for a side effect, says permanently when it cannot be undone, and never writes Warning or Caution.
  now: partly - Dialog has the shape, Title asking and Detail saying more (`feedback.go:385-386`, `feedback.go:568-575`), and Notice has Text and Detail (`feedback.go:227-228`); nothing checks the wording.
WRD-27 | Labels, buttons, menu items, tabs, titles, list items, prompts and main instructions end without a full stop; a question ends with a question mark wherever it is. Complete sentences in supplemental text and explanations end with a full stop (tooltips: WRD-13); status text is short fragments without one. One space between sentences. Double quotation marks around object names such as file names, not around paths, web addresses or names obvious from context. A colon introduces a list; use the serial comma; write and, or and number in words, not &, +, / or #. Emphasis only for what must not be missed: bold rarely, italics for a word mentioned as a word, never capitals.
  now: none - No punctuation check (`uitest/uitest.go:194-212` checks names only). TypeAhead quotes a new value with double quotation marks (`typeahead.go:406`).
WRD-28 | Be polite, calm and positive; never blame, talk down to or alarm the reader. In messages say problem, not error or failure; unable to or can't, not failed to; incorrect or not valid, not illegal, invalid or bad; stop, not abort, kill or terminate; serious, not fatal or catastrophic. Say please only when asking the reader to put up with something, sorry only for serious problems such as lost data, now or immediately only when it is urgent. Use the active voice and the present tense, contractions but not with names, and say what the reader can do rather than what they cannot.
  now: none - Not checked. The library's own messages avoid the words ("Not a number", "Must be at least N", `numberfield.go:109-113`).
WRD-29 | Labels of the options in one group (check boxes, radio buttons, list options, slider ends, answers) are parallel in form and similar in length, each distinct, and state only what differs: shared words go in the group label. Choosing an option turns something on (Don't show again is the accepted exception). A choice meaning none or all is in parentheses ((None)); a strongly recommended one adds (recommended) to its own label, an expert one (advanced); a unit goes in parentheses after the label (Size (MB)). A label is never half a sentence completed by a control (Remind me [5] minutes before), and text is never assembled from pieces at run time.
  now: none - RadioGroup takes Label and Detail per option without checks (`radiogroup.go:16-20`). Counts go through `UI.CountPhrase` rather than built phrases (`numbers.go:21-37`), but Stepper builds "Decrease "+Label (`stepper.go:66`) and Tag "Remove "+text (`marks.go:197`).
CTL-1 | One primary button per view, for the action the view is for; alternatives offered together are the same size and differ only in style.
  now: partly - "One primary per region" is the doc (`button.go:22-25`) but nothing enforces it.
CTL-2 | Choose the control by the choice: a checkbox for one on/off option whose off state is obvious, a switch for a setting with large scope that acts at once, radio buttons (stacked) for one of a few options worth the space, a select beyond that or to play a choice down, segmented for two to five short options. Values from data, numbers and choices changed often while working go in a list, select or number field, not radio buttons or checkboxes. A group holds at most ten checkboxes; when at least one must be ticked, an error says so.

Anything that shares information, changes the system or desktop, adds software or accepts legal terms is opt-in, with nothing preselected.
564	  now: partly - Theme follows the desktop (CON-5); the settings file holds only theme, interface size and typography (`settings/store.go`). Opt-ins are app matters, not covered.
565	OTH-5 | Design judgment: serve the product's purpose, make the few common features excellent, let people move freely, and let nothing slow the task. Start with the simplest design that works and remove every element and word the main tasks do not need; fix a confusing feature by redesigning it, not by putting a guided flow in front of it.
566	  now: none - Not a library matter.

now: none - No Find key and no search-field registration (survey §5); whether the field selects its text on focus is unison's field, not verified.
KEY-14 | A shortcut is taught where its command appears: every menu-bar item with a shortcut shows it, and a toolbar button's tooltip shows it too; context menus show none.
  W: All the shortcuts are also listed together on one help page.
  M: The general rule (CMD-11).
  now: partly - MenuItem.Key draws the shortcut (`menu.go:252-258`), but apps set it by hand; Field's tooltip shows its `Shortcut` (`field.go:154-164`); IconButton's tooltip has no shortcut (`iconbutton.go:69-74`).
KEY-15 | On Windows and Linux every interactive control has an access key: Alt and a letter underlined in its words or its label, unique in the window, which operates the control at once (only focuses it when shared). Every menu and menu item has one, unique within its level. Access keys and shortcuts are separate things.
  W: None on OK, Cancel and Close (Enter and Escape serve them; a button that means OK or Cancel under other words does get one), links, tabs (Ctrl+Tab), a plain Help button (F1), an ellipsis-only browse button, controls without words, toolbar items, group titles (unless keys run short) or static text. Commit buttons are assigned first with the standard letters (Y, N, the n of Don't, A for Apply), then the first letter or an early, wide, distinctive one (w, m, capitals; x in Exit), avoiding i, l and letters with or beside descenders. About 20 at most per dialog, leaving room for translation. Underlines show while Alt is held, or always when the system asks; Alt alone shows and focuses a hidden menu bar.
  M: None: macOS has no access keys, and the words are drawn without the marker, as Kvit's menus already do (`menu.go:21-24`).
  now: partly - Menus underline the `&` letter and choose by it while open (`menu.go:21-24`, `menu.go:525-564`); tray menus keep text plain (`platform/tray_windows.go:486`, `platform/tray_linux.go:445`); no control outside a menu has an access key, there is no Alt+letter route and no menu bar (survey §4).
PTR-1 | Clicks mean what they mean everywhere: a primary click selects or activates when the button is released over the target, so moving off abandons it; a secondary click opens the context menu; the wheel scrolls. A double-click is told from two clicks by the system's double-click speed, a double-click where only single clicks make sense counts as one, and clicks made while the app is busy count once.
  W: Only a customisable toolbar has a context menu, opened on right mouse down; a status-bar area answers only to a single left click and opens its menu on press. Tray icon: acts on release; a left click shows the likeliest view (a flyout, the settings or the main window), a right click the menu with its default command in bold, a double click runs that default. Timeouts scale from the system's double-click speed.
  M: The status-item menu opens on any click (`platform/tray.go:73-75`).
  now: partly - Controls act on release over their box (`control.go:122-151`) and Table rows on release over the same row (`tablebody.go:334-351`); right-click, the Menu key and Shift+F10 open the context menu (`window.go:103-109`, `menu.go:714-756`); tray lines have no default (`platform/tray.go:49-60`); the toolt
PTR-2 | The pointer shape says what will happen: arrow, I-beam over text, pointing hand over links, resize arrows over edges, not-allowed where a drop is refused. The pointer is never hidden, except in full-screen presentation, where it comes back as soon as the mouse moves.
  now: partly - Pointing, Arrow and Resize are used (`link.go:48`, `splitview.go:58-60`); no not-allowed or copy pointer; nothing hides the pointer.
PTR-3 | Support drag and drop where people will try it. Basic tasks never need a drag, double-click, right-click, modifier-click or hover: each has a visible command as well.
  now: partly - DualList is keyboard and buttons only by design (`duallist.go:11-17`); Table drags columns, not rows (`table.go:870-899`).
PTR-4 | A drop within a container moves; a drop into another container copies; when unsure, take the outcome that loses nothing.
  now: none - No drag and drop of content.
PTR-5 | While dragging, show what is dragged and how many, keep the pointer captured even outside the object, highlight only the target under the pointer that accepts it, and show a refused drop going back.
  now: partly - EmptyState `Dashed` draws a drop target (`emptystate.go:30-34`); nothing else.
PTR-6 | After a drop, the dropped items are selected where they landed and the drop can be undone; a drop that cannot be undone asks first.
  now: none - Not covered.
PTR-7 | Several selected items drag as one; one press-and-drag both selects and drags; dragging from an inactive window leaves its selection alone.
  now: none - Not covered.
PTR-8 | Fields accept typed, pasted and dropped input; a drop offers and takes the richest format both sides understand.
  now: partly - Fields paste through unison's editor (`field.go:19-21`); dropping is not handled.
PTR-9 | Clicking a column heading sorts by it and clicking again reverses; columns can be resized by dragging their dividers.
  now: enforces - Header press sorts or reverses (`table.go:459-477`); edge drag resizes (`table.go:858-861`).
PTR-10 | Clicking a disclosure triangle opens that node only; with the modifier it opens all below; a click on a selected name in an editable tree renames, a double click opens.
  now: partly - Tree expands and collapses by click and keys (`tree.go:299-366`); no expand-all.
PTR-11 | Controls that hide themselves come back when the pointer moves over their area.
  now: enforces - The sidebar rail opens on hover or keyboard focus (`window.go:132-161`).
PTR-12 | Hovering over text that is cut short shows the whole text.
  now: partly - Table cells and FloatingView titles disclose cut text (`tablebody.go:200-252`, `floatingview.go:194-208`); Label does not (survey §15).
PTR-13 | With a popover open, a click on another control that opens one closes the first and opens the second in one click.
  now: none - Not checked; outside clicks close the popover (`popover.go:114`).
PTR-14 | The whole visible target is clickable, its symbol and its words alike, and it sits near where it is used; when marks are too small to hit, the whole plot is the target and moving across it reads values.
  now: enforces - Controls take the press anywhere in their box (`control.go:122-151`); Trend has a hover crosshair (catalog KvitTrend).
PTR-15 | In a list, table or tree that allows several, a click selects one item, Shift-click extends to a range and the toggle modifier adds or removes one item. A double-click selects the item and runs its default command, which is also on a button or in the context menu.
  W: Ctrl-click toggles; Shift and Ctrl select the same way with the right button; a Shift- or Ctrl-double-click adjusts the selection and runs the default on all of it. In text a double click selects a word and a triple click the paragraph.
  M: Command-click toggles.
  now: partly - Table: Shift-click range and toggle-modifier click (`tablebody.go:296-306`), double press activates (`tablebody.go:343-346`); Tree selects one node and runs OnActivate on a double-click of a leaf (`tree.go:311-317`); no row context menu built in (survey §12).
A11Y-1 | Every element has a name a screen reader says, and the name is the words on screen, so voice control can use them. A control without words is named by what it does, in at most 150 characters, without "Click to": the role is spoken already.
  now: enforces - `uitest.CheckNamed` (`uitest/uitest.go:180-212`); IconButton's Label is name and tooltip (`iconbutton.go:23-27`).
A11Y-2 | No distinction rests on colour alone, nor on bold or italic alone: the words make sense in plain type.
  now: enforces - Library rule (CLAUDE.md, The library's rules; SKILL.md); a checked menu line is a tick as well as bold (`menu.go:40-42`).
A11Y-3 | Text and controls meet contrast minimums in every theme, including high contrast.
  now: enforces - Theme contrast floors (SKILL.md, Lines).
A11Y-4 | The interface works at every interface size: headings stay above body text, layouts reflow rather than clip, and information-carrying symbols grow with text.
  W: Also test at 100, 125 and 150 percent display scaling for clipped controls and text and stretched images.
  M: The general rule.
  now: enforces - Sizes are Measures read at layout time (CLAUDE.md).
A11Y-5 | Never carry meaning by sound or animation alone. Nothing flashes between 2 and 55 times a second; the app's sounds stay between 500 and 3000 Hz and follow the system's volume.
  now: enforces - Toast and ConfirmInPlace announce themselves (`feedback.go:120`, `confirminplace.go:122-131`); the library plays no sound and nothing it draws flashes.
A11Y-6 | Charts are readable by a screen reader: an overview of kind and axes, each mark named context first, series named by meaning, a sensible keyboard route through values.
  now: enforces - Data components give screen-reader phrasing (`data.go:146-148`, `data.go:606-612`).
A11Y-7 | Treat accessibility as a requirement and test with a screen reader, keyboard only and the system's accommodations.
  now: enforces - uitest gives a screen reader's view (CLAUDE.md).
A11Y-8 | What the screen shows, the screen reader gets: text is drawn as text (never inside a picture, built from characters or drawn over a progress bar); each label is tied to its control and never wraps around it as a sentence; a group shown by placement is declared as a group; and every focus change raises the event screen readers follow.
  now: partly - `uitest.CheckNamed` accepts LabeledBy but no component sets it (`uitest/uitest.go:207`); Progress draws its percentage beside the bar, not on it (`progress.go:70-77`); text is drawn by the `text` package; focus events are unison's (not verified).
CMD-1 | Every command the app has is in a menu of the menu bar, including ones also on toolbars, buttons and context menus, so every task can be found on screen rather than remembered.
  W: The menu bar belongs to the main window (Kvit-drawn) and is required for a main window with many commands in many categories. Windows 7 also lets a simple app hide it by default when its toolbar and direct commands cover nearly everything (hidden, never removed: Alt and a View > Menu bar check item bring it back), or do without one when it would hold three or fewer menus, using toolbar menu buttons, or a menu per task tab. Without a visible menu bar, the toolbar reaches every command not in the window or its context menus, and nothing expects people to reveal the hidden bar. Whether Kvit apps take that freedom is an open question (Q-1).
  M: Required: the system menu bar, always present.
  now: none - No menu bar and no command object (survey §4).
CMD-2 | Put the platform's standard menus in its standard order, leave out only the ones the app has no use for, and keep to at most ten menus, none holding only one or two items.
  W: File, Edit, View, the app's own menus, Tools, Help; no app menu and no Window menu; Options is the last item of Tools (WIN-16). A program that does not create or view documents may name and group its menus by its readers' tasks (Play, Library, Rip) instead. unison's per-window bar has File, Edit, Window, Help, with Exit in File and Preferences in Edit (unison `menu_bar.go:84-136`), so kvit-ui builds its own on Windows and Linux.
  M: App, File, Edit, Format, View, app menus, Window, Help.
  now: none - No menu bar (survey §4).
CMD-3 | About, the settings command and Quit or Exit sit where the platform puts them, with the same short app name; About holds the app's own facts, such as its version.
  W: No app menu: About <App> is the last item of Help after a separator (CMD-8), Options the last item of Tools (WIN-16), Exit the last item of File, its Alt+F4 usually not shown.
  M: The app menu holds About, Settings…, app-level configuration, Services, Hide, Hide Others, Show All and Quit, in that order.
  now: none - No menu bar and no About (survey §4, §11).
CMD-4 | The File menu holds the document commands in the platform's standard order, as the app needs them.
  W: New, Open…, Close; Save, Save as…; Send to; Print…, Print preview, Page setup; the numbered recent files inline; Exit (Alt+F4). Save as… saves under a name the reader gives, where the Mac offers Duplicate.
  M: New, Open, Open Recent, Close, Save, Duplicate, Rename…, Move To…, Export As…, Print…; Duplicate rather than Save As.
  now: none - No menu bar.
CMD-5 | The Edit menu starts with Undo and Redo, then Cut, Copy and Paste, Select all and Delete, then Find, in the platform's order; app-specific edit commands sit beside the standard ones they relate to.
  W: Undo, Redo (Ctrl+Y); Cut, Copy, Paste; Select all; Delete, Rename…; Find… (Ctrl+F), Find next (F3), Replace… (Ctrl+H), Go to… (Ctrl+G).
  M: Undo, Redo; Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Select All; Find; ending with the system's Dictation and Emoji items.
  now: partly - The field context menu has Cut, Copy, Paste, Select All and no Undo or Redo (`field.go:207-226`).
CMD-6 | The View menu holds the show and hide commands for the window's parts, zoom and full screen.
  W: Check items for the toolbars, the menu bar (how a hidden menu bar comes back), panes and the status bar; then Zoom in (Ctrl++), Zoom out (Ctrl+-), Text size; then Full screen (F11) and Refresh (F5).
  M: Show/Hide items and Enter Full Screen; window switching goes in the Window menu.
  now: none - The sidebar collapses to its rail by width only (`window.go:163-168`).
CMD-7 | On a Mac every app has a Window menu with Minimize, Zoom, the panels' show and hide items and the list of open windows.
  W: No Window menu: the standard Windows menus have none, and the taskbar switches windows.
  M: As stated.
  now: none - No menu bar.
CMD-8 | The Help menu is last; its first item opens the app's help, set apart from release notes and the like, and it stays short.
  W: <App> help (F1) first; after a separator, About <App> last. Product registration, if any, is a Help command and a link in the About box, never a step at first start.
  M: First item "<App> Help"; About is in the app menu.
  now: none - No menu bar, no help (survey §11).
CMD-9 | A main-menu item or toolbar button that cannot act now stays in place, disabled, and a menu whose items are all disabled still opens; only a menu that exists for one mode or selection drops the items that do not apply. Where working out whether an item can act would make the app noticeably slow, it stays enabled and says why when chosen.
  now: partly - Disabled lines are drawn and skipped (`menu.go:231-232`, `menu.go:298`); there is no toolbar, and nothing for a slow-to-check command.
CMD-10 | Every object and region with a few commands of its own has a context menu holding only the commands likely for what was clicked, in at most about four groups and 15 lines, leaving out those that do not apply except the standard clipboard ones; commands that everyone must find are also visible in the window or behind a visible menu button.
  W: Order: primary commands (Open, Run, Play, Print); the object's other commands; Cut, Copy, Paste; the object's settings; Delete, Rename; Properties last; separators between. The default command (what double-click or Enter does) comes first, marked bold. Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete and Rename, and the partner of a pair (Forward beside Back), stay in, disabled, when they do not apply. A list whose view, sorting or grouping can change offers View, Sort by and Group by submenus.
  M: Only Cut, Copy and Paste stay when they do not apply; no default item is marked.
  now: partly - Any panel can have one (`UI.SetContextMenu`, `menu.go:691-706`), opened by right-click, the Menu key or Shift+F10 (`menu.go:714-724`); it builds any list, with no default item and no length check.
CMD-11 | On a Mac a context menu shows no shortcuts; the main menus teach them.
  W: Shown, as in the other menus (the Windows 7 records say nothing against it; Kvit's field menu shows them, `field.go:211`).
  M: No shortcuts in context menus.
  now: contradicts - The field context menu passes each action's KeyBinding (`field.go:211`).
CMD-12 | Submenus only where they clearly help, one level deep, about five items at most; three or more items sharing a leading word become one submenu.
  W: No submenus in a context menu at all. Windows 7 allows a rare second level in the main menus; Kvit keeps one level, which satisfies both.
  M: A submenu in a context menu where it clearly helps, as in other menus.
  now: partly - Submenus nest without limit (`menu.go:50-54`).
CMD-13 | Order a menu by its natural sequence where it has one (steps of a task, numbers in numeric order), otherwise most used first; group related items between separators, at most seven to a group (a submenu counts as one) and about 25 to a level; a rare command stays in its group, and a command sits in one menu only unless it truly belongs in two.
  now: none - Menus take any list (`menu.go:19-55`).
CMD-14 | Give a menu item a symbol only when it clarifies the item, and then the same symbol everywhere the command appears.
  now: partly - Symbols are dropped on macOS menus (`menu.go:119-148`), which suits this rule there.
CMD-15 | Mark an option that is on; mark the chosen one of exclusive options in the platform's way; where attributes combine, one item clears them all.
  W: A tick for an independent on/off option; a bullet for the chosen one of a set of mutually exclusive options (at least two in the set); no mark when the option is on for only part of the selection.
  M: A tick for both; a dash when the option is on for only part of the selection.
  now: partly - A tick for Checked (`menu.go:40-42`, `menu.go:236-239`); no bullet or mixed form, and Select marks its option with Checked (`select.go:96`).
CMD-16 | Holding a modifier never silently changes what a dialog button does. In a Mac menu a modifier may reveal an alternate command, which then also exists another way, uses one modifier, and never appears in a context or tray menu.
  W: No alternates revealed by a modifier, in menus or dialogs: they cannot be discovered (XP's Yes to All turning into No to All). Offer the variant as its own item.
  M: Alternates in the menu bar's menus, as stated.
  now: enforces - MenuItem has no alternate (`menu.go:19-55`), so the Windows form holds and the Mac form is not offered.
CMD-17 | A menu button lists at least three commands that refine its own action; variants of one command go in a split button whose main part runs the likeliest variant (or the last one chosen, when people repeat it), marked in its menu; one or two commands are buttons, and a view's main actions are visible, not in a menu. Simple choices (check or radio items, a short list) may sit in a menu rather than a dialog.
  now: none - No split button or menu button component; Select is a single-choice list (`select.go`).
CMD-18 | Toolbars, menu bars and status bars belong to main windows; dialogs have none. A toolbar holds the commands for the main tasks, mostly single-click buttons that act at once, each recognisable at a glance and shown once, in at most three groups; property buttons show and change the state of the selection; commands or a whole toolbar for one mode or selection show only while it is active; a button's words never change while the app runs, only its symbol may show state.
  W: Commands start at the leading edge; Help, and the standard Options and View commands, sit at the trailing end. Beside a menu bar a toolbar button takes the immediate form of a command (Print prints at once) and leaves the asking form (Print…) to the menu; a toolbar standing in for the menu bar takes the asking form.
  M: At most one primary action, at the trailing end; navigation and critical actions get their own group.
  now: none - No toolbar component; ViewHead and Header carry actions (catalog KvitViewHead, KvitHeader).
CMD-19 | When a toolbar does not fit, its lower-priority items move, in a set order, into a More menu that exists only then; every command stays reachable.
  now: partly - StatusBar overflows into "N more" (`statusbar.go:288`); nothing else does.
CMD-20 | Let people choose which toolbar items show when there are many or the app is used for long sessions; customisation starts locked, can be reset to the original, and the settings command is not a toolbar item.
  W: No Customize command beside Options: customisation is reached from Options. A customisable toolbar starts locked; its context menu lists the toolbars as check items, Lock the toolbars, and Customize…; the customisation window has Reset.
  M: View > Customize Toolbar…, the system's customisation sheet.
  now: none - Not covered.
CMD-21 | No on-screen buttons for Cut, Copy and Paste; undo and redo buttons only where they are really needed, with the standard symbols.
  now: none - Not covered.
CMD-22 | Show text on a button when a word or two says more than a symbol; use a symbol for a familiar action; never type letters or punctuation as a stand-in for a symbol.
  now: none - Not covered; the symbol set lacks bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, code and heading (catalog Symbols).
CMD-23 | A destructive command in a menu sits last, after a separator, marked as destructive, and asks before running unless it can be undone (MSG-3).
  now: partly - MenuItem.Danger exists; the separator is the caller's job (`menu.go:35-39`).
CMD-24 | A tray icon (Windows, Linux) or Dock menu (macOS) serves an app that works in the background: the icon shows its status and is not a launcher, and its menu lists the open windows and a few actions useful with no window open, each also in the menu bar or a window.
  W: The menu opens at the icon: Open (the default, bold) and Run; a separator; ticked toggles (Suspend and Resume for background work, Minimize to tray, notification opt-ins, Display icon in notification area); a separator; Options and Exit. Exit quits for this session and removes the icon; no About unless the app has no window. A click on the icon may open a light flyout: a summary matching the tooltip, the common tasks and settings applied at once, closed by a click outside. Minimise to the tray only when the reader opts in, for a long-running single-instance app, and only through Minimize, never Close. A hidden icon comes back only from Options.
  M: The Dock menu; a menu bar extra, where there is one, opens its menu on any click (`platform/tray.go:73-75`).
  now: partly - The tray menu has Text, Separator, Disabled and OnSelect only (`platform/tray.go:49-60`), with no default or check items; OnClick exists except on macOS (`platform/tray.go:73-75`).
CMD-25 | Offer printing as deep as the kind of app needs: Print… in the File menu only when there is something to print, through the system's print dialog, showing only the options that apply; a document editor also offers a preview.
  W: Print… opens the dialog; a toolbar Print button beside a menu bar prints one copy at once to the default printer, named in its tooltip; without a menu bar Print is a split button offering Print…, Print preview and Page setup. Print preview shows margins, page breaks, orientation, headers and footers, pages through the document and prints from it. Within a session the next job keeps the printer and paper size but not the copies or page range.
  M: Print… opens the system print panel, whose preview serves; no separate preview command is needed.
  now: none - No printing in kvit-ui.
WIN-1 | Dialog buttons follow the platform's order and placement.
  W: Commit buttons form one right-aligned row at the bottom, even a lone OK, never centred; left to right: OK or [Do it] or Yes, [Don't do it] or No, Cancel, Apply, Help.
  M: Default button at the trailing end, Cancel just before it (leading side of the pair).
  now: contradicts - The confirming button is on the right on every system (`feedback.go:371`, `feedback.go:541-552`).
WIN-2 | An alert asks one question, with a specific title, explanatory text only when it adds something, and at most three buttons; a routine or informational message that can recur offers a don't-show-again option, while an error or a necessary warning never does: if it seems to need one, it should not be shown.
  W: Worded "Don't show this <item> again" (Don't show this reminder again), or "Don't show this message again" for a dialog in general.
  M: The alert's suppression checkbox, "Do not show this message again" unless the app words it.
  now: partly - Dialog has Title, Detail and two buttons at most (`feedback.go:382-417`); it has no don't-show-again option.
WIN-3 | Every dialog that offers a destructive action has Cancel, and Cancel is never the default; a sheet or step with Done also has Cancel or Back; a dialog whose answers are command links keeps a separate Cancel button, never a cancelling link.
  now: partly - A destructive dialog focuses Cancel (`feedback.go:470-479`); nothing stops an empty CancelText.
WIN-4 | Mark a confirming button as destructive only when the destruction is a side effect the reader may not expect; a deliberate Empty Trash or Overwrite is not marked.
  now: partly - Dialog.Destructive exists (`feedback.go:390-392`); when to use it is not said.
WIN-5 | Use a modal dialog only for a short task that must be answered first; long work, tools used alongside the window and find-and-replace go in a window, a panel or a popover.
  now: enforces - Dialog's own doc says it is "expensive, and worth it only where the answer really does come first" (catalog KvitDialog).
WIN-6 | A modal view has a title naming its task and an obvious way out inside it, with nothing else looking like the close control; the close control means Cancel or Close, never OK.
  W: Every dialog has the title bar's Close (Kvit draws it beside the title), never disabled except in a progress dialog that must finish to avoid losing data. A dialog with settings also has Cancel in its body, a modeless one Close. The title names the command, feature or program it came from (a progress dialog the operation), never what to do; the question goes in the main instruction (MSG-4).
  M: Alerts and sheets have no close control; the way out is Cancel or Escape.
  now: partly - Three ways out: close symbol, Cancel, Escape (`feedback.go:368-375`), the close symbol rejecting as Cancel does (`feedback.go:428-429`); the close symbol shows on macOS too, and Title asks the question (`feedback.go:385-386`) where the Windows form names the command.
WIN-7 | One modal at a time: close a dialog before opening another, except that an alert may sit over a dialog, and on Windows a helper dialog over its owner; at most one popover, none opened from inside another.
  W: A dialog may open a helper over itself (a chooser, a settings window it owns); the owner stays open underneath and the helper closes first.
  M: As stated.
  now: none - Popups stack without a check (`layer.go:58-68`).
WIN-8 | Cancel discards a dialog's or flow's input without asking; closing it would throw away significant effort, or by a route people may take for OK (the close control after many changes), first says so and offers to keep it.
  now: contradicts - Dismissal is always a decline (`feedback.go:498-504`), with nothing to keep typed input.
WIN-9 | A dialog that belongs to one window blocks only that window and stays with it; the app's other windows stay usable, and bringing a window forward raises only it and the windows it owns, which restore with it.
  now: enforces - The modal scrim is per window (`layer.go:80-99`).
WIN-10 | A popover closes on a click outside and keeps what was entered; a single-choice popover closes when the choice is made; Cancel and Done appear only when they clarify whether changes are kept; a tray icon's popup applies its settings at once.
  now: enforces - Popover closes on Escape and outside click (`popover.go:114`).
WIN-11 | Every main window can be resized, moved and minimised in the system's frame, which shows whether it is active and holds no app controls; it opens at a size that shows its typical content, has a minimum size where its content stops working, drops optional parts below that rather than squeezing them, and its layout works at every size above it.
  W: Every resizable window can be maximised and restored, to its largest useful size when it gains nothing from more. It fits and works on an 800×600 screen less the taskbar, and its default layout aims at 1024×768 (LAY-3's open question on the window floor). The title bar's right-click window menu is the system's.
  M: Zoom and the system's full-screen mode (WIN-15).
  now: partly - System frame; minimum size Px(880)×Px(600) (`window.go:88-92`), above Windows' 800×600 floor at larger interface sizes; no full screen (survey §9).
WIN-12 | A window's title names its content and tells it apart from the app's other windows; a new document is Untitled until named.
  W: A document window: "document name - program name"; another main window: the program name; a dialog: the command or feature that opened it; a properties window "<name> Properties" ("<first>, … Properties", or Selection Properties, for several). A window on the taskbar puts what tells it apart first (66% Complete, 3 Reminders). A window that shows its name prominently inside may hide the caption, but still sets the title.
  M: The document or place, without the app's name.
